newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Sale of Venezuela banks heralds new era.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sale of Venezuela banks heralds new era.

text.p: The auction of two leading Venezuelan banks, plus the surprise sale of a 40 percent stake in the country's largest, heralds a new era of competition in the country's financial sector, analysts said on Thursday.
"It's very positive that major foreign players are entering the market.... It strengthens the sector and opens up a whole new ball game," CNI financial consultant Frank Amador said.
In a surprise announcement, Spain's Banco de Bilbao Vizcaya said it bought a 40 percent share in Venezuela's leading bank, Banco Provincial.

"BBV has reached an agreement with Empresas Polar and Credit Lyonnais to control 40 percent of Banco Provincial," the bank said in a statement released in Madrid. The statement did not say how much BBV would pay for the stake.
Separately, Fogade, the national state deposits guarantee fund, sold 90 percent of Venezuela's second largest-bank Banco de Venezuela to Spanish bank Santander for $338.4 million.
Fogade also sold 80 percent of Banco Consolidado to Chilean financial group Infisa for $123.5 million, although Infisa may finally pay $143.75 million for a 93 percent share.
The sales of those two banks "have made it possible for us to realize our dreams," said Fogade President Esther de Margulis at the public presentation of the bidding results.
Infisa representative Manuel Balbontin later said in Caracas: "Our entry, along with Santander's, will prove a great advance for Venezuela's banking sector and the Venezuelan consumer."
Total revenues from the Banco Venezuela sale will reach an estimated $376.38 million, Margulis said, and $154.4 million for Consolidado.

Those figures include popular share offerings designed to sweeten the sale and quell nationalistic concerns. Local investors placed orders for 10.28 percent of Banco de Venezuela, worth 13.8 billion bolivars ($29.4 million), and some eight percent of Consolidado, worth some five billion bolivars ($10.5 million), Margulis said.
The new banks' owners are expected to force modernization and greater efficiency on Venezuela's undeveloped retail banking system.
"It certainly raises the question of what strategies the other banks should follow in this new market," Amador said.
Many consider Venenzuela's banking system overextended and still fragile after a 1994-95 financial crisis absorbed an estimated $11 billion in state bailouts.
"In many ways this a closing of the loop and the financial crisis," Amador said.
